::: {#task .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-studio-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> three rewritten questions, each with an audience, a metric with units and a <span class="lx-term" data-term="counterfactual">counterfactual</span>, and one question card for the best of them.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> twenty illustrative questions about energy systems, which you sort and type first.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> your card reaches Proficient on Framing: a typed question with audience, metric with units, counterfactual, scale and boundary, and one <span class="lx-term" data-term="falsification-statement">falsification statement</span>.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 30 minutes guided here, then about an hour on your own: collect ten questions from your courses, your work or the news, sort and type them, and turn the best into a card.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="r01-framing" data-src="../assets/learn/data/r01-framing.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The four bins</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Researchable:</b> specific, still open, and answerable with data you could get.</li>
<li><b>Too vague:</b> no metric, no audience or no comparison.</li>
<li><b>Already answered:</b> a lookup in a public dataset, or settled physics.</li>
<li><b>Not answerable with the data at hand:</b> the data the question names cannot show the answer.</li>
</ul>
<!-- r01-task:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>The twenty questions, sorted, with reasons</summary>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Question</th><th scope="col">Where it goes</th><th scope="col">Why</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>In 2025, how many hours did Prairie Town's wind output stay below a tenth of its maximum, season by season?</td><td>Researchable · descriptive</td><td>Specific and answerable: the town's hourly 2025 wind data can be counted by season. Descriptive: it asks how often, not why.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Is solar power good?</td><td>Too vague</td><td>Good for whom, measured how, compared with what? No audience, metric or comparison.</td></tr>
<tr><td>How much electricity did the United States use in 2025?</td><td>Already answered</td><td>EIA publishes it: about 4.20 trillion kWh. A lookup, not a study; why use changed could be one.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Did a co-op's time-of-use tariff cut its members' evening peak demand, compared with similar co-ops that kept flat rates?</td><td>Researchable · evaluative</td><td>A named programme, a metric and a comparison group. Evaluative: it judges a past change against a comparison.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Using only each state's yearly electricity sales, at what hour of the day do electric-vehicle owners charge?</td><td>Not answerable with the data at hand</td><td>Yearly totals cannot show hours. Hourly charger or feeder data could.</td></tr>
<tr><td>What mix of rooftop solar and batteries should a school district buy to keep its 20-year cost lowest, compared with grid supply alone?</td><td>Researchable · prescriptive</td><td>A decision-maker, a metric and a comparison, with public prices and tariffs to work from. Prescriptive: it asks what a decision-maker should do.</td></tr>
<tr><td>How can we fix the grid?</td><td>Too vague</td><td>Fix what: outages, prices, emissions? Which grid, and who would act?</td></tr>
<tr><td>Why did heating demand fall more in some neighbourhoods than in others after the same retrofit programme?</td><td>Researchable · explanatory</td><td>An observed difference to explain, with meter and building data to test the reasons. Explanatory: it asks why an observed difference happened.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Does a battery give back less energy than it takes in?</td><td>Already answered</td><td>Yes: every charge and discharge loses some energy (round-trip efficiency, lesson 9). How much one battery loses can still be measured.</td></tr>
<tr><td>During a week-long cold snap, how would all-electric heating change the risk of elderly households losing heat, with and without backup?</td><td>Researchable · predictive</td><td>A stated event, a group, a risk to estimate and two cases to compare. Predictive: it asks what would happen under a stated event, with uncertainty.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Where in Prairie City are rooftop solar systems concentrated, compared with median household income by neighbourhood?</td><td>Researchable · descriptive</td><td>Specific and answerable from permit records and census income data. Descriptive: it maps where, without asking why.</td></tr>
<tr><td>What is the future of energy storage?</td><td>Too vague</td><td>No place, period, metric or audience: a topic, not a question.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Using one year of a utility's outage records, how will its customers' outage hours change by 2060?</td><td>Not answerable with the data at hand</td><td>One year cannot separate a trend from a bad year, and 2060 needs scenarios as well as records.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Did a rural co-op's community-solar programme lower renters' energy burden more than bill credits of the same cost would have?</td><td>Researchable · evaluative</td><td>A programme, a metric and a fair counterfactual: the same money spent another way. Evaluative: it judges a past programme against an alternative.</td></tr>
<tr><td>What was the average capacity factor of U.S. utility-scale wind farms in 2025?</td><td>Already answered</td><td>EIA reports it: 33.8% (Electric Power Monthly). Why regions differ could be a study.</td></tr>
<tr><td>What will Prairie City's winter peak demand be in 2035 if half its homes switch to heat pumps, and with what range?</td><td>Researchable · predictive</td><td>A stated change, a metric with units and a range to estimate. Predictive: it asks what a future value will be, with uncertainty.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Are heat pumps worth it?</td><td>Too vague</td><td>Worth what, to whom, over how long, compared with which heating?</td></tr>
<tr><td>Which pumping schedule should a Plains farm adopt to cut its power bill under the co-op's time-of-use tariff without lowering yield?</td><td>Researchable · prescriptive</td><td>A decision, a goal and a limit, with the tariff and pump data to work from. Prescriptive: it asks what the farm should do.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Using Prairie Town's hourly grid demand alone, why did each household's electricity use change?</td><td>Not answerable with the data at hand</td><td>Town-level demand mixes thousands of homes; household changes need meter data or a survey.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Why did some rural co-ops' customers lose power for longer than their neighbours' in the same ice storm?</td><td>Researchable · explanatory</td><td>An observed difference, with outage records and line data to test the reasons. Explanatory: it asks why the same storm had different effects.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Three vague questions, rewritten as examples</summary><ul>
<li><strong>“Is solar power good?”</strong> became: Did the co-op's community-solar array lower members' average yearly bill, compared with buying the same energy at wholesale prices? <em>Evaluative.</em> Audience: the co-op's board, which decides whether to build a second array. Metric: average bill per member ($ a year). Compared with: the same energy bought at wholesale prices.</li>
<li><strong>“Are heat pumps worth it?”</strong> became: Over 15 years, would a cold-climate heat pump cost a Prairie Town homeowner less than a new gas furnace? <em>Predictive.</em> Audience: homeowners replacing a furnace, and the town's rebate office. Metric: net present cost of heating ($ over 15 years). Compared with: a new gas furnace installed at the same time.</li>
<li><strong>“How can we fix the grid?”</strong> became: Which would cut Prairie Town's customer outage hours more per dollar over ten years: a second feeder or a battery at the substation? <em>Prescriptive.</em> Audience: the co-op's engineering committee. Metric: customer outage hours avoided per $1 million spent (hours per $ million). Compared with: today's single feeder, with no upgrade.</li>
</ul></details>
<!-- r01-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you sort and rewrite step by step, and your drafts stay in this browser.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><span>The twenty questions, the rewrites, the co-ops, Prairie Town and Prairie City are illustrative. Two answers quote public numbers, U.S. electricity use in 2025 and the 2025 wind capacity factor, with their sources at the end of the page.</span></p>
```
:::

::: {#exemplars .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Two answers to the same task
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r01-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<p>Turn “Is community solar good for low-income families?” into a question card.</p>
<!-- r01-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak answer · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Question: Is community solar good for low-income families [1]?
Type: not named [2]
Audience: low-income families
Metric: savings [3]
Compared with: (blank) [4]
Scale and boundary: rural areas [5]
I would be wrong if: (left blank) [6]</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> “Good” is not a metric: any result could be read as success.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> Without a type, a survey, a model and a regression could all claim to answer it.</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> No units and no period: dollars a month, or a share of income, over which years?</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> No <span class="lx-term" data-term="counterfactual">counterfactual</span>: savings compared with what?</li><li value="5"><b>Falls short:</b> A place, not a <span class="lx-term" data-term="system-boundary">boundary</span>: which programme, which members, which years, and what is left out?</li><li value="6"><b>Falls short:</b> No falsification statement: no result could show the expectation wrong.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong answer · Proficient</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Question: Did a rural co-op's community-solar programme lower renters' energy burden more than bill credits of the same cost would have?
Type: evaluative [1]
Audience: the co-op's board [2]
Metric: energy burden, yearly energy bills as % of household income [3]
Compared with: bill credits of the same total cost [4]
Scale and boundary: S1 community; the co-op's renter members, 2022–2025; landlords' costs left out [5]
I would be wrong if: participants' burden fell no more than that of similar renters given credits [6]
Main uncertainty: renters who moved away during the four years</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Names the type: a past programme judged against a comparison.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> Names who would act on the answer.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> A metric with units that bills and income data can compute.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> The counterfactual spends the same money another way, so the comparison is fair.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> Says who and which years are counted, and what is left out.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> Names the result that would show the expectation false.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak answer</th><th scope="col">Strong answer</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Type</th><td>Not named</td><td>Evaluative</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Audience</th><td>Those affected</td><td>Those who decide</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Metric and units</th><td>“Savings”, no units</td><td>Bills as % of income</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Counterfactual</th><td>None</td><td>Credits of the same cost</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Boundary</th><td>“Rural areas”</td><td>Members, years, what is left out</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Falsification</th><td>None</td><td>A result that would show it wrong</td></tr></tbody></table>
<!-- r01-exemplars:end -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Four tests before a question is worth researching</p>
<ol>
<li>Specific? If not, it is too vague: rewrite it.</li>
<li>Already answered by a public dataset or settled physics? Then use the answer, and ask what is still open.</li>
<li>Can the data at hand show the answer? If not, change the data or narrow the question.</li>
<li>Then it is researchable: name its type.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#selfcheck .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check your own work against the rubric
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r01-rubric" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The question card</p>
<p>Write one sentence ending in a question mark, then its type, audience or decision-maker, metric and units, counterfactual, scale and boundary, “I would be wrong if…”, and the uncertainty that matters most. With JavaScript on, a card form checks each part.</p>
<!-- r01-rubric:start (written by LX.Rubric's staticHTML, from the course rubric, and from the data file's checklist, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts lx-rb-static"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Competence</th><th scope="col">Developing</th><th scope="col">Proficient (the bar)</th><th scope="col">Strong</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Framing<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: your card passes all eight checks, and its boundary says what is left out.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Question vague or untyped; no audience or counterfactual.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Typed question with audience or decision-maker, metric with units, counterfactual, scale and boundary; one falsification statement.</td><td data-l="Strong">Also explains why the question matters to its audience and what answer would change a decision.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">A checklist to reuse</p>
<ul><li><b>One sentence:</b> About one system and one period, ending in a question mark.</li><li><b>Typed:</b> Descriptive, explanatory, evaluative, predictive or prescriptive.</li><li><b>Audience:</b> Someone who would act on the answer, or read it.</li><li><b>Metric with units:</b> Something you could measure or compute, such as <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-burden">energy burden</span> in % of income.</li><li><b>Counterfactual:</b> What happens otherwise: the baseline you compare with.</li><li><b>Still open:</b> Not a lookup in a public dataset, and not settled physics.</li><li><b>Answerable:</b> Data you can get show the effect, at the time step it needs.</li><li><b>Falsifiable:</b> You can name a result that would show you wrong.</li></ul>
<!-- r01-rubric:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="r1-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="novel" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A question is worth researching only if nobody has written about it.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Novelty can be a new question, new evidence, a new place or a new mix of methods, and it has to survive a literature search (<a href="r02-literature.html">R2</a>).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="optim" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A ‘what should … do?’ question needs an <span class="lx-term" data-term="optimization">optimization</span> model.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Optimization is one way. Decision analysis and multi-criteria methods also answer prescriptive questions (<a href="r03-system-and-method.html">R3</a> compares the families).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="data" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If the data at hand cannot answer a question, the question is useless.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Change the data, with meter readings or a survey, or narrow the question; a good question can outlive one dataset.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cf" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Naming the <span class="lx-term" data-term="counterfactual">counterfactual</span> is part of framing, not an extra.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Every effect is measured against something; without a stated comparison, almost any result can be read as success.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>From a card to a proposal</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>In the research capstone (CR, upcoming), your proposal opens with this card. <a href="r10-question-studio.html">R10</a>, the question studio, helps you generate candidate questions; <a href="r02-literature.html">R2</a> tests what is already known; <a href="r03-system-and-method.html">R3</a> picks the system, the boundary and the method.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Sorting is a judgement: a few questions sit near a border, and a mentor may place them differently. The reasons matter more than the bins.</li>
<li>The studio checks the form of a question, not whether it matters. Whether it matters is a conversation with the people who would use the answer.</li>
<li>The twenty questions are illustrative and tidy; real ones arrive half-formed, and the same rewriting applies.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

